To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
non-biodegradable, but not biodegradable plastic and N deposition reduced plant survival probability and growth, and plastic and N interacted in affecting plant growth.

non-biodegradable and biodegradable (but not degradable) plastics, and elevated nitrogen deposition, reduce the colonization success of vegetative propagule of dune plants, and that biodegradable plastic and elevated nitrogen deposition could favour the colonization of generalist species, such as Sporobolus pumilus, over dune-building species, such as Thinopyrum junceum, with negative consequences for the functioning of these coastal ecosystems.
plastic litter and elevated N deposition reduce vegetative colonization of dune plants and that biodegradable plastics may further threaten coastal dune ecosystems by favouring generalist plants.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of two major anthropogenic drivers of biodiversity loss on plant communities of a coastal habitat of global conservation concern.
two global environmental problems, namely plastic pollution and increased atmospheric N deposition.
the effects of plastic litter and elevated N on plant colonization success and growth, and the role of plant-plant interactions in mediating these effects.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the plastic pollution is a further threat to the coastal ecosystems.

plastic litter is a further threat to beach-dune systems by reducing plant colonization, and that biodegradable plastic, in addition to non-biodegradable, could be a further threat by affecting vegetative recruitment and growth of dune plants.

plastic and N deposition have the potential to alter the structure of plant communities of coastal dunes, and that biodegradable plastic and N deposition could favour non dune-building species and hinder dune-building species.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
plastic pollution is a further threat to coastal habitats.
the combined effects of biodegradable plastic litter and increased N deposition can alter plant community composition, with consequences for ecosystem functioning.
plastic litter and N deposition are major threats for the future of coastal dune habitats.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, when plastic is deposited on coastal ecosystems, its effects on plant colonization and growth are not only negative but also highly variable and species-specific, depending on plastic type and biotic conditions.

, when considering the combined effects of plastic and N deposition on dune plants, it is important to consider the biotic context and the ecological role of species, and to focus not only on shoot but also on root and rhizome biomass.
the combined effect of plastic and N on plant colonization success and growth is species specific and mediated by plant-plant interactions.
